subject: ss-paediatric-cardiology
title: Paediatric Cardiology
examPattern: NBEMS NEET-SS Paediatric Group. 150 questions (100 questions in 2024+ bulletin). Feeder: MD/DNB Paediatrics. All questions are feeder-speciality content covering General Paediatrics and all Paediatric Super-Specialities.
books: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 22e Vol 2, Part XVIII (The Cardiovascular System, Chapters 469-493)
Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 22e Vol 1 (Chapter 130 Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn; Chapter 208 Kawasaki Disease)

lessonTopics.title: Fetal Circulation and Physiological Shunts

mustKnow.fact: Ductus venosus shunts 50-60% of oxygenated umbilical venous blood directly into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the hepatic microcirculation.
Crista dividens directs high-oxygen blood from the inferior vena cava preferentially through the foramen ovale into the left atrium.
Ductus arteriosus diverts approximately 90% of right ventricular output from the pulmonary artery into the descending aorta.
Endogenous prostaglandin E2 and low fetal oxygen tension maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus in utero.
First breath causes lung expansion and oxygenation, dropping pulmonary vascular resistance by 80% within the first postnatal minutes.
Functional closure of the ductus arteriosus occurs within 10-15 hours after birth in healthy term neonates via smooth muscle constriction.
Anatomical closure of the ductus arteriosus forms the ligamentum arteriosum, completed by 2-3 weeks of life.
Alprostadil infusion at 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min maintains ductal patency in duct-dependent congenital cardiac lesions.

lessonTopics.title: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN)
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Nelson 22e Vol 1 Chapter 130 & Vol 2 Chapters 470 and 472

mustKnow.fact: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn results from failure of normal postnatal drop in pulmonary vascular resistance, causing right-to-left extrapulmonary shunting.
A right radial (pre-ductal) to lower limb (post-ductal) arterial oxygen saturation difference greater than 10% confirms ductal right-to-left shunting.
In the hyperoxia test with 100% inspired oxygen, PaO2 remaining below 100 mmHg suggests cyanotic congenital heart disease rather than parenchymal lung disease.
Inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm is the specific first-line pulmonary vasodilator for term and late preterm neonates with refractory hypoxemia and oxygenation index exceeding 25.
mustKnow.source: AAP Committee on Fetus and Newborn

mustKnow.fact: Oxygenation index is calculated as Mean Airway Pressure multiplied by FiO2 multiplied by 100 divided by post-ductal PaO2.
Oral or intravenous sildenafil selectively inhibits phosphodiesterase-5 to augment cyclic GMP-mediated pulmonary vasodilation in PPHN.
Intravenous milrinone provides phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition to improve right ventricular function and reduce pulmonary arterial afterload.
Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is indicated when oxygenation index exceeds 40 despite maximal medical therapy.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Electrocardiography: Normal Values and Chamber Enlargement

mustKnow.fact: Normal neonates exhibit physiological right ventricular dominance with right axis deviation (+110 to +180 degrees) and prominent R waves in lead V1.
The T wave in lead V1 is upright for the first 48-72 hours of life, then inverts and remains normally inverted until 6-8 years of age (juvenile T-wave pattern).

mustKnow.term: Abnormal upright T wave in V1
mustKnow.fact: An upright T wave in lead V1 between 7 days and 6 years of age is a reliable indicator of right ventricular hypertrophy.
Pediatric RVH criteria: R wave in V1 or S wave in V6 exceeding the 98th percentile for age, or pure R wave in V1 > 10 mm in infants.
LVH criteria: R wave in V6 or S wave in V1 exceeding 98th percentile for age, or presence of Q waves > 4 mm in V5-V6 or inverted T waves in V6.
P pulmonale is defined as peaked P waves exceeding 2.5 mm in lead II in any pediatric age group.
P mitrale features broad, notched P waves with duration >= 0.08 s in infants or >= 0.10 s in older children, with biphasic P in V1 having deep negative terminal deflection.
PR interval varies with age and heart rate, normally 0.08-0.12 s in infants and increasing to 0.12-0.16 s in adolescents.

lessonTopics.title: Diagnostic and Interventional Pediatric Cardiac Catheterisation

mustKnow.fact: Cardiac output is calculated by Fick formula: Oxygen Consumption (VO2 in mL/min) divided by arteriovenous oxygen difference (CaO2 - CvO2).
Pulmonary flow (Qp) to systemic flow (Qs) ratio: Qp/Qs = (Systemic arterial O2 sat - Mixed venous O2 sat) / (Pulmonary venous O2 sat - Pulmonary arterial O2 sat).
An oxygen saturation increase >= 7-8% between right atrium and right ventricle confirms a left-to-right ventricular shunt; >= 9-10% from SVC/IVC to RA confirms an atrial shunt.
Femoral artery thrombosis occurs in up to 3-5% of infants undergoing arterial catheterisation, treated with systemic heparinization or tissue plasminogen activator (tPA).
Pediatric catheterization radiation mitigation uses pulsed fluoroscopy (3-7.5 pulses/second), low-dose detector settings, and strict collimation.
mustKnow.source: AHA Scientific Statement on Radiation in CHD

mustKnow.fact: Ductal occlusion using Amplatzer duct occluders is contraindicated in neonates with active sepsis, severe pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunt, or duct-dependent systemic lesions.
Balloon angioplasty is the intervention of choice for native coarctation in older children and recoarctation post-surgery, with covered stenting preferred in adolescents > 35 kg.
Normal resting left ventricular end-diastolic pressure in children is 6-12 mmHg; values > 15-18 mmHg indicate elevated left-sided filling pressures.

sections.title: Acyanotic Congenital Heart Disease and Shunts

modules.title: Acyanotic Shunts and Obstructive Lesions: VSD, ASD, PDA and Coarctation

lessonTopics.title: Ventricular Septal Defect: Anatomy and Haemodynamics

mustKnow.fact: Perimembranous VSD accounts for 70-80% of all defects, located in the membranous septum adjacent to the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve.
Muscular VSDs account for 5-20% and have the highest spontaneous closure rate of up to 80% during infancy.
Infundibular (subpulmonic / doubly committed) VSD carries a high risk of aortic regurgitation due to right coronary cusp prolapse, warranting early surgical closure regardless of shunt size.
A harsh holosystolic or pansystolic murmur is heard best at the lower left sternal border; smaller defects produce louder murmurs (maladie de Roger).
A pulmonary to systemic flow ratio (Qp:Qs) exceeding 1.5 indicates a hemodynamically significant left-to-right shunt.
Initial medical management of congestive heart failure in large VSD combines loop diuretics such as furosemide 1-2 mg/kg/day with an ACE inhibitor such as captopril.
Irreversible pulmonary vascular obstructive disease with shunt reversal from left-to-right to right-to-left usually develops after 12-24 months of age in untreated large defects.
Surgical patch closure is indicated before 6-12 months of age in infants with failure to thrive, intractable heart failure, or pulmonary hypertension.

lessonTopics.title: Atrial Septal Defects and Endocardial Cushion Defects

mustKnow.fact: Ostium secundum ASD accounts for 70% of all atrial septal defects and has a female to male predilection of 2:1.
Ostium primum ASD occurs low in the atrial septum as part of an endocardial cushion defect and is consistently associated with a cleft anterior mitral valve leaflet.
Sinus venosus ASD is situated near the SVC or IVC junction and is strongly associated with partial anomalous pulmonary venous drainage (PAPVD).
The classic auscultatory hallmark of an ASD is wide and fixed splitting of the second heart sound with a systolic ejection murmur at the second left intercostal space.
Ostium primum defect characteristically exhibits left axis deviation and counterclockwise superior QRS loop on vectorcardiography, whereas secundum ASD displays right axis deviation and rSR prime.
Secundum ASD with adequate rims of at least 5 mm from adjacent cardiac structures is amenable to transcatheter closure using an Amplatzer septal occluder.
Complete atrioventricular septal defect is the most common cardiac anomaly in Down syndrome (trisomy 21), accounting for 40-50% of defects in these patients.
Elective transcatheter or surgical closure of an uncomplicated hemodynamically significant secundum ASD is recommended between 3 and 5 years of age.

lessonTopics.title: Patent Ductus Arteriosus: Preterm and Term Presentations

mustKnow.fact: Classic Gibson murmur of PDA is a continuous, rough, machinery-like murmur peaking around S2, best heard at the left infraclavicular area and second left intercostal space.
Rapid diastolic run-off from the high-pressure aorta into the low-pressure pulmonary circulation causes wide pulse pressure and bounding water-hammer pulses.
In extremely low birth weight infants weighing under 1000 g, hemodynamically significant PDA occurs in over 50-70% of neonates.
Cyclooxygenase inhibitors including indomethacin (0.2 mg/kg), ibuprofen (10 mg/kg initial followed by 5 mg/kg), or paracetamol (15 mg/kg every 6 hours) achieve ductal closure in preterm infants.
Ibuprofen demonstrates equal efficacy to indomethacin with significantly lower risk of necrotizing enterocolitis and renal impairment.
Maternal first-trimester rubella infection is classically associated with persistent patent ductus arteriosus and peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis.
Percutaneous transcatheter closure using coils or duct occluders is the standard treatment for term infants and older children weighing above 5-6 kg.
When severe pulmonary hypertension reverses PDA shunt right-to-left, differential cyanosis occurs with cyanosis of lower limbs but pink normal upper extremities.

lessonTopics.title: Coarctation of the Aorta: Neonatal and Childhood Forms

mustKnow.fact: Coarctation is most frequently located just distal to the left subclavian artery opposite the ductus arteriosus insertion (juxtaductal).
A systolic blood pressure gradient exceeding 20 mmHg between the upper right arm and lower extremities establishes the diagnosis of significant coarctation.
Simultaneous palpation of radial and femoral pulses reveals marked diminution and delay of the femoral pulse.
Inferior rib notching (Roesler sign) affects the 3rd to 8th ribs due to dilated collateral intercostal arteries, rarely seen in children under 5 years of age.
CXR demonstrates a figure of 3 contour on the left upper mediastinal border, matched by the reversed E sign on barium swallow.
Bicuspid aortic valve coexists with coarctation of the aorta in 50-85% of cases.
Coarctation of the aorta occurs in up to 15-20% of females with Turner syndrome (45,X karyotype).
Critical neonatal coarctation presents with cardiogenic shock and anuria upon ductal closure, requiring immediate prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) infusion.

lessonTopics.title: Valvular Aortic Stenosis and Pulmonary Stenosis

mustKnow.fact: Valvular pulmonary stenosis is the most common form of right ventricular outflow obstruction, accounting for 8-10% of all congenital cardiac defects.
Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis with PTPN11 gene mutation is the hallmark cardiovascular anomaly of Noonan syndrome in 50-60% of patients.
Percutaneous balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty is the definitive treatment of choice for moderate to severe pulmonary stenosis when the peak Doppler gradient exceeds 40-50 mmHg.
Bicuspid aortic valve is the most frequent congenital anomaly of the aortic valve, with a male-to-female ratio of 3:1 to 4:1.
Aortic stenosis severity by echocardiography: mild when mean gradient is under 25 mmHg, moderate between 25-40 mmHg, and severe when peak gradient exceeds 50-64 mmHg or mean gradient exceeds 40 mmHg.
Aortic stenosis produces an early systolic ejection click at the apex that does not vary with respiration, unlike the pulmonary ejection click which softens on inspiration.
The Ross operation replaces the diseased aortic valve with the patient's own pulmonary autograft, with a homograft placed in the pulmonary position.
Supravalvular aortic stenosis caused by elastin gene (ELN) deletion on chromosome 7q11.23 is the pathognomonic lesion of Williams syndrome.

sections.title: Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease and Single Ventricle

modules.title: Cyanotic Heart Defects: TOF, TGA, TAPVC, Truncus and HLHS

lessonTopics.title: Tetralogy of Fallot: Anatomy and Pathophysiology

mustKnow.fact: The four classic components of Tetralogy of Fallot result from anterocephalad deviation of the infundibular septum: large subaortic VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, and RV hypertrophy.
The severity of subpulmonic and valvular right ventricular outflow obstruction determines the magnitude of right-to-left shunt and degree of cyanosis.
CXR classically shows a boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) with upturned apex due to right ventricular hypertrophy and a concave pulmonary bay.
A right-sided aortic arch is present in approximately 25% of patients with Tetralogy of Fallot.
Microdeletion of 22q11.2 (DiGeorge / velocardiofacial syndrome) occurs in 15% of isolated TOF and up to 40-50% of TOF with pulmonary atresia or absent pulmonary valve.
Children with TOF learn to squat during exertion to increase systemic vascular resistance, thereby decreasing right-to-left shunting and promoting pulmonary blood flow.
The murmur in TOF is caused solely by RVOT stenosis (systolic ejection murmur at mid-to-upper left sternal border); the VSD is large and non-restrictive (silent).
The second heart sound is typically single because the pulmonary component (P2) is markedly delayed and inaudible.

lessonTopics.title: Hypercyanotic Spells and Surgical Repair of TOF

mustKnow.fact: Hypercyanotic or Tet spells are triggered by crying, feeding, or defecation causing increased infundibular spasm and sudden drop in systemic vascular resistance.
Immediate non-pharmacological management is the knee-chest position, which kinks the femoral arteries and abruptly increases systemic afterload.
Subcutaneous or intravenous morphine sulphate at 0.1-0.2 mg/kg calms the infant and suppresses the respiratory drive to break the cycle of hyperpnoea.
Intravenous propranolol (0.01-0.1 mg/kg) or esmolol relieves infundibular spasm and slows heart rate during refractory spells.
Intravenous phenylephrine (5-20 mcg/kg bolus) selectively stimulates alpha-1 receptors to elevate systemic vascular resistance and force blood through the RVOT.
The modified Blalock-Taussig shunt connects a systemic artery (subclavian) to the ipsilateral pulmonary artery using a synthetic Gore-Tex tube graft as palliation.
Elective complete primary repair (VSD closure and RVOT reconstruction) is ideally performed between 3 and 6 months of age in developed centres.
Transannular patch repair carries a long-term risk of free pulmonary regurgitation leading to right ventricular dilatation, requiring pulmonary valve replacement (PVR).

lessonTopics.title: Ebstein Anomaly and Tricuspid Atresia

mustKnow.fact: Ebstein anomaly features downward apical displacement of the septal and posterior leaflets of the tricuspid valve by at least 8 mm/m2 body surface area.
Apical displacement partitions the right ventricle into a thinned, dysfunctional atrialised portion and a small functional right ventricle.
Extreme cardiomegaly producing a wall-to-wall heart appearance on chest radiography occurs from severe tricuspid regurgitation and huge right atrium.
First-trimester intrauterine exposure to lithium carries an increased relative risk of Ebstein anomaly in the fetus.
Accessory conduction pathways producing WPW pattern and SVT occur in up to 20-30% of patients with Ebstein anomaly, predominantly right-sided pathways.
Tricuspid atresia features complete agenesis of the tricuspid orifice, requiring an obligatory ASD for right-to-left systemic venous mixing and a VSD or PDA for pulmonary blood flow.
Tricuspid atresia is the single major cyanotic congenital heart defect with left axis deviation and left ventricular hypertrophy on infant ECG.
Tricuspid atresia cannot support a biventricular circulation and undergoes staged univentricular palliation culminating in the Fontan procedure.

lessonTopics.title: D-Transposition of the Great Arteries (D-TGA)

mustKnow.fact: D-TGA features ventriculoarterial discordance where the aorta arises from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, creating two parallel, independent circulations.
Survival requires communication between circuits via a patent ductus arteriosus, atrial septal defect, or ventricular septal defect.
CXR classically demonstrates an egg-on-a-string cardiac silhouette due to narrow superior mediastinal shadow from anteroposterior great vessel alignment and thymic involution.
Balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) is performed percutaneously or bedside under echocardiographic guidance to create a large unrestrictive interatrial communication.
The arterial switch operation (Jatene procedure) is the definitive anatomical correction of choice, transecting and switching the great vessels with coronary artery reimplantation.
The arterial switch operation must be performed within the first 2-3 weeks of life in intact ventricular septum before left ventricular mass regresses.
Congenitally corrected transposition (L-TGA) features both atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance, where the systemic ventricle is the morphologic right ventricle.
Spontaneous complete atrioventricular block develops at a rate of approximately 2% per year throughout life in ccTGA due to an elongated, abnormal conduction bundle.

lessonTopics.title: Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC)

mustKnow.fact: Darling classification divides TAPVC into Type I Supracardiac (45%), Type II Cardiac (25%), Type III Infracardiac (20-25%), and Type IV Mixed (5%).
Supracardiac TAPVC draining to a persistent left vertical vein, innominate vein, and right SVC produces the classic snowman or figure-of-8 contour on chest radiograph.
Type III infracardiac TAPVC drains below the diaphragm into the portal system and is almost always severely obstructed, presenting on day 1 with severe pulmonary venous congestion and shock.
An unrestrictive atrial septal defect is mandatory to allow systemic cardiac output from the fully mixed right atrium into the left atrium.
Complete mixing in the right atrium results in identical oxygen saturation values across all four cardiac chambers and great vessels.
Obstructed TAPVC is a true surgical emergency; balloon septostomy does not relieve the pulmonary venous obstruction and immediate surgical anastomosis to the left atrium is required.
Type II cardiac TAPVC drains directly into the coronary sinus, producing marked coronary sinus dilation on echocardiography.
Recurrent pulmonary vein stenosis occurs in 10-15% of postoperative patients and represents the most lethal late complication.

lessonTopics.title: Truncus Arteriosus and Single Great Vessels

mustKnow.fact: Persistent truncus arteriosus features a single common arterial vessel arising from the heart that supplies the systemic, pulmonary, and coronary circulations.
The truncal valve is dysplastic with 1 to 6 cusps (most commonly tricuspid or quadricuspid) and exhibits insufficiency in 20-30% of patients.

Collett and Edwards classification: Type I has a short pulmonary trunk branching into PAs; Type II has separate PAs arising close together from dorsal truncus; Type III has PAs arising from lateral sides.
Van Praagh type A4 incorporates coarctation or interrupted aortic arch with large patent ductus arteriosus.
Over 30-40% of truncus arteriosus cases have chromosome 22q11.2 microdeletion (DiGeorge syndrome).
Complete repair is performed in the first month of life using a patch to close the VSD (committing LV to truncus) and an RV-to-PA valved homograft conduit.
Significant truncal valve regurgitation requires concomitant truncal valvuloplasty or replacement during neonatal repair.
Massive run-off from the truncus into low-resistance pulmonary arteries during diastole produces wide pulse pressure and bounding peripheral pulses.

lessonTopics.title: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome: Anatomy and Norwood Staging

mustKnow.fact: HLHS encompasses aortic atresia/stenosis, mitral atresia/stenosis, hypoplastic diminutive left ventricle, and severe hypoplasia of the ascending aorta.
Systemic circulation is entirely ductus-dependent, with right ventricular blood traversing the PDA retrograde into the aortic arch to perfuse coronaries and cerebral vessels.
Norwood Stage 1 performed in the first week creates an unobstructed neo-aorta using pulmonary trunk, atrial septectomy, and systemic-to-pulmonary shunt (modified BT or Sano RV-PA conduit).
The Sano modification uses a non-valved PTFE conduit from the RV to PA bifurcation, eliminating systemic diastolic steal and preserving coronary perfusion.
Bidirectional cavopulmonary shunt (Glenn procedure) anastomoses the superior vena cava directly to the right pulmonary artery at 4-6 months of age.
Extracardiac conduit total cavopulmonary connection (Fontan) routes IVC blood to pulmonary arteries at 2-4 years, completing passive single ventricle venous return.
A 4-5 mm fenestration between the Fontan conduit and atrium acts as a pop-off valve to maintain systemic cardiac output at the cost of mild cyanosis.
Protein-losing enteropathy and plastic bronchitis are severe late complications of chronically elevated central venous pressure in failing Fontan physiology.

sections.title: Arrhythmias, Myocardial and Acquired Heart Disease

lessonTopics.title: Supraventricular Tachycardia in Infants and Children

mustKnow.fact: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is the most common sustained symptomatic pathological arrhythmia in infants and children, with heart rates typically 220-300 bpm in infants.
Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT) mediated by an accessory pathway accounts for over 70% of SVT cases in infants, followed by AVNRT in older children.
Application of an ice bag to the upper face for 10-15 seconds (diving reflex) without compressing the orbits is the first-line vagal maneuver for hemodynamically stable infants.
Adenosine 0.1 mg/kg rapid IV push via a proximal vein followed by rapid flush is first-line pharmacological treatment, doubling to 0.2 mg/kg if needed (maximum single dose 12 mg).
Synchronized electrical cardioversion at 0.5-1 J/kg (increasing to 2 J/kg if ineffective) is indicated immediately for unstable SVT with poor perfusion or shock.
Intravenous verapamil is strictly contraindicated in infants under 1 year of age due to severe risk of refractory hypotension, electromechanical dissociation, and cardiac arrest.
Propranolol (2-4 mg/kg/day) or flecainide (50-100 mg/m2/day) is used for long-term oral suppression of recurrent SVT in infants.
Radiofrequency or cryoablation of accessory pathways is definitive therapy, typically deferred until the child reaches 15 kg or 4-5 years of age unless medically refractory.

lessonTopics.title: Long QT Syndrome, Brugada and Channelopathies

mustKnow.fact: The Schwartz diagnostic score incorporates QTc prolongation, torsades de pointes, syncope, congenital deafness, and family history (score >= 3.5 = high probability).
QTc calculated via Bazett formula is abnormal when exceeding 450 ms in males, 460 ms in females, and severely prolonged above 500 ms (high risk of sudden death).
LQT1 (KCNQ1 gene, IKs potassium channel) is triggered by physical exertion and swimming; responds excellently to beta-blockers.
LQT2 (KCNH2/HERG gene, IKr channel) is triggered by sudden auditory stimuli (alarms, ringing phones) and emotional stress.
LQT3 (SCN5A gain-of-function mutation, sodium channel) causes events during rest or sleep, treated with mexiletine alongside beta-blockers.
Autosomal recessive LQTS with bilateral profound sensorineural hearing deafness caused by homozygous KCNQ1 or KCNE1 mutations.
Non-selective beta-blockers nadolol (1-1.5 mg/kg/day) or propranolol are first-line therapy for all diagnosed LQTS patients regardless of symptoms.
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is indicated for survivors of cardiac arrest or those with recurrent syncope despite optimal beta-blocker therapy.

lessonTopics.title: Congenital Complete Heart Block and Bradyarrhythmias

mustKnow.fact: Congenital complete atrioventricular block strongly correlates with transplacental passage of maternal anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB autoantibodies.
Maternal systemic lupus erythematosus or Sjogren syndrome carries a 2% risk of neonatal heart block in first pregnancy, rising to 15-20% in subsequent pregnancies.
Sustained fetal ventricular heart rate below 50-55 bpm or hydrops fetalis indicates high risk of intrauterine demise.
mustKnow.source: AHA Scientific Statement on Fetal Arrhythmias

mustKnow.fact: Maternal administration of fluorinated corticosteroids (dexamethasone 4 mg/day) may arrest progression in incomplete or second-degree heart block but does not reverse complete block.
Class I indication for permanent pacemaker implantation in congenital complete heart block includes symptomatic bradycardia, ventricular escape under 50-55 bpm, or wide QRS.
Epicardial pacing systems are placed in infants weighing under 10-15 kg to avoid venous occlusion and lead stretching with growth.
Postoperative complete AV block resolving within 7-10 days can be monitored; persistence beyond 7-10 days mandates permanent pacemaker implantation before discharge.
Failure of ventricular rate to increase appropriately during exercise testing in older children with congenital block indicates need for pacing.

lessonTopics.title: Dilated, Hypertrophic and Restrictive Cardiomyopathies

mustKnow.fact: DCM is the most common pediatric cardiomyopathy (50-60%), caused by genetic mutations (sarcomeric, dystrophin), myocarditis, and inborn errors of metabolism.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is predominantly autosomal dominant caused by sarcomeric protein gene mutations: MYH7 (beta-myosin heavy chain) and MYBPC3.
Transient asymmetric septal hypertrophy occurs in 10-20% of infants of diabetic mothers due to fetal hyperinsulinemia; regresses spontaneously by 6-12 months.
Pediatric HCM sudden cardiac death risk factors: extreme LV wall thickness >= 30 mm (or Z-score >= 6), unexplained syncope, non-sustained VT, and family history of SCD.
Digoxin, positive inotropes, and vasodilators are contraindicated in obstructive HCM because they increase the dynamic left ventricular outflow tract gradient.
RCM is the rarest pediatric cardiomyopathy (< 5%) with the poorest prognosis (50% mortality at 2 years), characterized by marked biatrial enlargement and normal ventricular dimensions.
LVNC is characterized by prominent myocardial trabeculations and deep intertrabecular recesses, with non-compacted to compacted ratio > 2.0:1 in end-systole (Jenni criteria).
First-line neurohormonal blockade in pediatric dilated cardiomyopathy combines ACE inhibitors (enalapril), beta-blockers (carvedilol), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone).

lessonTopics.title: Acute Pediatric Myocarditis and Inflammatory Heart Disease

mustKnow.fact: Enteroviruses (coxsackievirus B), adenovirus, parvovirus B19, and human herpesvirus 6 are the most commonly identified viral triggers of acute myocarditis in children.
Cardiac troponin I and T are elevated in over 80% of children with acute myocarditis and serve as sensitive biomarkers of active cardiomyocyte necrosis.
mustKnow.source: AHA Scientific Statement on Pediatric Myocarditis

mustKnow.fact: Updated Lake Louise MRI criteria require both myocardial edema (T2 mapping / increased signal) and non-ischemic myocardial injury (T1 mapping, extracellular volume, or late gadolinium enhancement).
Endomyocardial biopsy histological diagnosis (Dallas criteria) requires myocardial inflammatory cellular infiltrate associated with myocyte degeneration and necrosis.
High-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) at 2 g/kg over 24-48 hours is widely used in acute pediatric myocarditis for immunomodulatory effects.
mustKnow.source: AHA Scientific Statement on Pediatric Myocarditis

mustKnow.fact: Milrinone is preferred over pure alpha-agonists due to inodilator properties reducing afterload while improving myocardial contractility without excessive tachycardia.
Venoarterial ECMO provides crucial hemodynamic rescue for fulminant myocarditis, with survival to discharge exceeding 70-80% due to potential for complete myocardial recovery.
Complete cessation of competitive sports and vigorous physical activity for at least 3 to 6 months is mandated following acute myocarditis.

lessonTopics.title: Pericarditis, Pericardial Effusion and Cardiac Tamponade

mustKnow.fact: Beck triad of cardiac tamponade comprises systemic hypotension, muffled or distant heart sounds, and elevated jugular venous distension.
Pulsus paradoxus is defined as an exaggerated inspiratory decrease in systolic arterial blood pressure exceeding 10 mmHg during normal breathing.

Key echocardiographic indicators of tamponade include early diastolic collapse of the right ventricle, late diastolic collapse of the right atrium, and reciprocal respiratory inflow variations across valves > 25-40%.
Beat-to-beat alternation of QRS complex amplitude and axis on ECG (electrical alternans) reflects swinging of the heart within a large pericardial effusion.
A symmetrical, globular, water-bottle appearance on chest radiograph requires at least 200-250 mL of pericardial fluid to manifest in older children.
Pericardiocentesis via subxiphoid approach under continuous echocardiographic and ECG monitoring is life-saving in cardiac tamponade.
Stage 1 ECG in acute pericarditis shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression across limb and precordial leads (except aVR and V1 which show PR elevation).
First-line medical treatment of acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis combines NSAIDs (ibuprofen) with weight-adjusted colchicine for 3 months to prevent recurrences.

modules.title: Rheumatic Fever, Infective Endocarditis and Kawasaki Disease

lessonTopics.title: Acute Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease

mustKnow.fact: AHA 2015 revised Jones criteria distinguish low-risk from moderate-to-high risk populations; diagnosis requires 2 major criteria OR 1 major plus 2 minor criteria alongside evidence of preceding Group A Streptococcus infection.

In moderate/high-risk endemic populations, major criteria include carditis (clinical or subclinical by Doppler echo), monoarthritis or polyarthritis, polyarthralgia, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules.
Sydenham chorea may present after a prolonged latent period of 1 to 6 months post-streptococcal pharyngitis and does not require streptococcal serological proof.
Mitral regurgitation is the single most common valvular lesion in acute rheumatic carditis (90%), followed by aortic regurgitation.
A short, soft, mid-diastolic murmur at the apex caused by increased flow across an inflamed, oedematous mitral valve during acute carditis.
Aspirin (50-60 mg/kg/day up to 80-100 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses) is indicated for arthritis; oral prednisolone (1-2 mg/kg/day for 2-3 weeks) is indicated for moderate-to-severe carditis.
Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (600,000 units for <= 27 kg; 1,200,000 units for > 27 kg) administered every 3-4 weeks is the gold standard secondary prophylaxis.

Duration of secondary prophylaxis: without carditis = 5 years or until age 21 (whichever longer); with carditis but no residual valve damage = 10 years or until age 21; with persistent valvular disease = 10 years or until age 40.

lessonTopics.title: Kawasaki Disease: Criteria, Aneurysms and Refractory Disease

mustKnow.fact: Fever for at least 5 days plus 4 of 5 features: bilateral non-exudative bulbar conjunctivitis, oral changes (strawberry tongue, cracked red lips), polymorphic rash, extremity changes (erythema, induration, periungual desquamation), and cervical lymphadenopathy (> 1.5 cm).
In infants under 6 months with unexplained fever >= 7 days, incomplete KD must be investigated with CRP >= 30 mg/L or ESR >= 40 mm/hr and supplemental laboratory criteria.
Single infusion of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) at 2 g/kg administered over 10-12 hours within the first 10 days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm risk from 25% to under 4%.
Oral aspirin is given at high dose (30-50 mg/kg/day in 4 doses) during the febrile phase, reduced to low antiplatelet dose (3-5 mg/kg/day) once afebrile for 48 hours until 6-8 weeks post-onset.

Coronary artery dimensions adjusted for body surface area: dilation = Z-score 2.0 to < 2.5; small aneurysm = 2.5 to < 5.0; medium aneurysm = 5.0 to < 10.0; giant aneurysm = Z-score >= 10.0 or absolute lumen >= 8 mm.
Persistent or recrudescent fever >= 36 hours after completion of the first IVIG infusion defines IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease (occurs in 10-20% of cases).
Treatment of IVIG-resistant KD entails a second dose of IVIG (2 g/kg) or high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone pulses (30 mg/kg/day for 3 days) or infliximab (5 mg/kg).
Live viral vaccines (measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella) must be postponed for 11 months following high-dose IVIG administration due to interference from passive antibodies.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Infective Endocarditis and SBE Prophylaxis

mustKnow.fact: Definitive clinical diagnosis requires 2 major criteria, 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria; echocardiography and persistently positive blood cultures are major criteria.
Viridans group streptococci (Streptococcus mitis, oralis) and Staphylococcus aureus are the two predominant pathogens causing infective endocarditis in children with congenital heart disease.

Antibiotic prophylaxis is restricted only to high-risk lesions: prosthetic cardiac valves/material, previous infective endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic CHD, repaired CHD with residual defects, or within 6 months of repair.
Single oral dose of amoxicillin 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) administered 30-60 minutes prior to invasive dental procedures manipulating gingival tissue.
For patients with severe immediate-type penicillin allergy, cephalexin (50 mg/kg), azithromycin (15 mg/kg), or clarithromycin (15 mg/kg) is recommended.

Initial empiric therapy for native valve endocarditis in children combines ampicillin (200 mg/kg/day) or ceftriaxone with gentamicin (3 mg/kg/day), adding vancomycin if methicillin-resistant S. aureus is suspected.

Surgical valve repair or replacement is indicated for persistent vegetation > 10 mm associated with embolic events, severe valvular regurgitation with refractory heart failure, or perivalvular abscess.
Classic immunological and vascular stigmata (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, splinter hemorrhages) are present in under 10-15% of children with infective endocarditis.

modules.title: Pediatric Pulmonary Hypertension and Heart Failure

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: Classification and Targeted Therapies

mustKnow.fact: Updated World Symposium definition of pulmonary arterial hypertension: mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) > 20 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure <= 15 mmHg, and pulmonary vascular resistance index (PVRI) >= 3 Wood units.m2.

Acute vasoreactivity testing during cardiac catheterisation with inhaled nitric oxide (20-40 ppm): positive response is a drop in mPAP >= 10 mmHg to an absolute mPAP <= 40 mmHg with preserved or increased cardiac output.
Only acute vasoreactive responders (approx 10-15% of pediatric idiopathic PAH) are candidates for high-dose oral calcium channel blocker therapy (nifedipine, diltiazem).
Oral sildenafil (0.5-1 mg/kg three times daily) or tadalafil acts via nitric oxide-cGMP pathway to selectively relax pulmonary arterial vascular smooth muscle.
Bosentan (dual ETA/ETB antagonist) and ambrisentan (selective ETA antagonist) block endothelin-mediated vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling; require monthly liver function monitoring.
Intravenous epoprostenol, subcutaneous or IV treprostinil, or inhaled iloprost are indicated for high-risk, severe, or WHO functional class IV pediatric PAH.

Surgical Potts shunt (side-to-side anastomosis between left pulmonary artery and descending aorta) or balloon atrial septostomy decompresses the failing right ventricle, acting as a bridge to lung transplant.
Corrective closure of congenital cardiac shunts is strictly contraindicated once irreversible pulmonary vascular resistance index exceeds 8 Wood units.m2 with right-to-left shunting.
